### I. The Geography of Drift

The house at Cape Vane was built not to withstand the water, but to negotiate with it. It stood upon a knuckle of black basalt where two counter-rotating tides met twice daily in a white, boiling seam, tossing whatever the world had dropped into the trough between them. The locals—what few remained three miles inland, behind the wall of wind-twisted tamaracks—called the spit *The Teeth*, though there was nothing predatory about it. It was simply an obstacle against which the sea unloaded its pockets.

The house itself had been erected in the late nineteenth century by an eccentric hydrographer named Julian Finch, whose son, Alistair, had inherited both the structure and its purpose. When Alistair died in the middle of his seventy-eighth winter, he left no will, no living kin, and thirty-four rooms packed from floor to lintel with flotsam. 

I was hired by an obscure testamentary trust in Edinburgh whose clerks seemed genuinely embarrassed by the estate’s existence. My instructions, typed on legal vellum that smelled faintly of damp cellar, were terse: *To assess, classify, and prepare a definitive inventory of the material remains, distinguishing between items of historical or pecuniary interest and common refuse.*

Common refuse. The phrase could only have been written by someone who had never seen what thirty years of salt water does to an iron padlock, or how the belly of a green demijohn turns iridescent when rolled for a century across the crushed shells of the Dogger Bank.

I arrived in late October, when the daylight was already retreating like grease drawn back from the center of a hot pan. Maro, a man with the scarred, purplish knuckles of a crabber, dropped me at the edge of the shingle with two wooden crates of tinned mutton, six gallons of kerosene, and a bundle of dry kindling.

"The roof in the west scullery gives when the wind comes from the Minch," he told me, not looking at my face, but at my boots, which were new, yellow leather, entirely unsuited for the slate-slick ramps of the Cape. "Keep the chimney damper half-shut or the stove will smoke you blind. I’ll come on the new moon with flour and oil. If you aren't on the slipway, I’ll assume you’ve fallen off the shelf and leave the sacks above the high-water mark."

He pushed his skiff back into the grey chop before I could thank him, his oars working with that flat, rhythmic economy born of knowing that the water does not care whether you hurry or drown.

The house was cold with a coldness that felt structural, as though the stones had been quarried from ice. I did not light the main lamps that first evening. I built a small, snapping fire in the grate of what had once been the morning room, set up my canvas field cot between two stacks of tea chests containing hundreds of rubber boot-soles—all for the left foot, all marked with the diamond tread of a firm in Bristol that ceased trading before the Great War—and slept to the heavy, sliding crash of the beach stones moving in their beds.

***

### II. The Taxonomy of the Lost

Alistair Finch had not been a collector; collectors are governed by pride, by the desire to possess the complete set, the rarest stamp, the unblemished specimen. Finch had been an archivist of severance. 

In the four hundred-odd notebooks I discovered during my first fortnight—octavo ledgers bound in oilcloth, their pages warped into stiff, yellow ribbons by the humidity—he had laid down his rules of acquisition. He accepted nothing that had been discarded intentionally.

*“A bucket thrown over the gunwale because its stave is split,”* he wrote in May of 1964, *“is merely garbage. It has completed its narrative; its owner has agreed to its death. But a bucket lost because a painter parted in a gale off the Faroes remains suspended. It is a word dropped from a sentence before the clause was finished. It carries the momentum of an interrupted intention.”*

It was this interrupted intention that he sought to document. 

His system of classification was entirely non-Linnaean, based neither on material nor date of manufacture, but on what he termed *The Degree of Relinquishment*. 

Room Four, for example, contained only things that had slipped through fingers: horn-handled pocketknives, thimbles of pressed nickel, copper pennies worn so flat they resembled fish scales, spectacles without frames, bone buttons, and fountain-pen caps. He had laid them out on trestle tables covered in green baize, each anchored by a slip of parchment bearing the date and wind direction of its discovery. 

*Item 1,402: Comb of tortoiseshell, three teeth remaining. Recovered 14 November 1971. South-southwest gale. Trace of lavender pomade in the spine.*

*Item 1,403: Silver signet ring, crest worn illegible by sand-friction. Found in the throat of an anglerfish washed up at the low ebb. 3 December 1971.*

I spent my mornings with a wooden calipers and a brass balance scale, measuring the breadth and mass of these casualties. In the afternoons, when the light failed—which happened shortly after three—I sat by the iron stove and transcribed his ledger entries into my own clean, cold ledgers, erasing his wilder marginalia to make the text acceptable to the lawyers in Edinburgh.

Yet, after three weeks of this, the boundary between Finch’s madness and my own labor began to blur. 

One finds oneself alone in a house where the walls are lined with twenty thousand objects that once touched a palm, a lip, a pocket, and one begins to hear them. Not as voices—the dead are never that polite—but as a low, collective drag, like the sound of gravel pulled down a slope by the backwash.

In the second week of November, I came upon the room he had designated *The Hall of Unsent Letters*.

It occupied the former ballroom, a long, high-ceilinged gallery whose plaster cornices were weeping salt-damp in long, yellowish trails. Here, Finch had suspended strings of catgut from wall to wall, three feet apart, from the floor to the height of a man’s shoulder. Clamped to these strings with wooden clothes-pegs were several thousand sheets of paper, dried seaweed-brown, translucent, folded, ripped, or sealed in wax that had been chewed by crabs into grey lace.

There were bills of lading from ships that had foundered before the telegraph was strung; fragments of ledgers from timber barques out of Archangel; pages torn from Bibles carried by cabin boys who had never learned to swim; and hundreds of scraps of private correspondence, salvaged from oilskin pouches, waterlogged sea-chests, or found simply pasted by the spray against the rocks like wet leaves.

I unpegged one at random. The ink had faded to the color of dried tea, but the handwriting was round and firm—the hand of a schoolmistress or a clerk’s daughter:

*“…and if the herring do not show by Michaelmas, my father says we must give the cottage to the factor and go down to Greenock. I have kept the ribbon from your bonnet under my shift, though it smells of nothing now but the coal-smoke from the hearth. Write to me through the smith at Kilmory. Do not write to the house…”*

The remainder of the sheet had been dissolved by water or eaten by the small, translucent lice that live beneath drift-logs. There was no name, no year, no address. There was only the ribbon, which had presumably decayed seventy years ago, and the woman who had carried it, who was now earth herself, and the man at sea who had never received the instruction to avoid writing to the house.

I held the scrap between my fingers. The paper was crisp, salted into parchment. If I dropped it into the stove, it would flare for two seconds and leave a flake of grey ash no larger than an almond. Who would be wronged by its disappearance? The court in Edinburgh wanted to know if there were paintings, first editions, silverplate, or deeds to land. They did not want three square inches of someone’s girl telling someone’s boy that the herring had failed.

I should have swept it into the zinc bin. Instead, I laid it between two pieces of glass, taped the edges, and set it upon the table beside my own tobacco tin.

***

### III. The Salt Archive

By December, the weather had closed down like an iron trap. Maro came once, his dory leaping like a horse across the grey swells, his face lashed red by sleet. He did not come ashore; he merely brought the boat close enough to the slippery timber of the pier to toss two sacks of oats, a tin of dried yeast, and three boxes of salt beef onto the deck before hauling his sheet and falling away with the tide.

"Stay off the lower shingle!" he shouted through his cupped hands, his voice thin against the thrum of the wind. "The shelf is cutting out! The drift is coming in deep!"

I did not ask what he meant by *the drift coming in deep*. I knew already.

For a week, the wind had been blowing from the north-northeast, dragging the great polar water down through the gaps between the islands. At night, the house shuddered with a frequency that matched the long Atlantic rollers. In my bed, beneath three horsehair blankets and my wool greatcoat, I could feel the impact through the stone foundations: a thud that traveled up through the spine of the rock, through the floorboards, into the iron frame of the cot, shaking my heart against my ribs.

In the mornings, the beach had changed its face.

A storm on that coast is not a removal; it is an addition. The tide does not take away; it disgorges. It vomited up fields of kelp whose stalks were as thick as a man’s thigh, black and shining like rubber pipes; it threw up timbers of Norwegian spruce, splintered as though by siege-engines, their iron bolts turned to spikes of orange rust; it cast up the plastic debris of our own century, those bright, unrotting toys, bleach bottles with Spanish labels, crates from fish-packing plants in Halifax, nylon nets that had drifted across the pole like strangling veils.

Finch had spent the last decade of his life dealing with this modern flotsam, and his notes on it were marked by a profound, clinical disgust.

*“The ocean used to cast up bones,”* he had written in 1898, in the small, trembling script of his last months. *“Wood, horn, linen, wool, iron. Things that had been born of the earth and were slowly being unmade by the brine, returning by degrees to their elements. Now it casts up things that cannot die. They are not dead; they were never alive. They are the ghosts of oil. They will lie upon these stones when the sun has grown red and cold.”*

In the cellars of the house, where the water seeped through the mortar and stood three inches deep in the floor-gutters, he had arranged his collection of modern detritus: thousand upon thousand of plastic oil containers, sun-bleached to the color of bone; monofilament lines tangled like the hair of suicides; and, most strangely, hundreds of rubber bath toys—yellow ducks, blue frogs, pink pigs—which had been spilled from a container ship in the mid-Pacific in the early nineties and had circled the Arctic basin for five years before finding their way down the spout between Cape Vane and the mainland.

He had arranged them in rows on shelves made of driftwood, their painted eyes rubbed away by the pumice of the sand, their bills slightly parted in identical, molded smirks. 

They were utterly terrifying. They had crossed the roof of the world without a crew, without a thought, preserved in their bright, petrochemical innocence through months of pack-ice and months of midnight sun, to sit at last in this dark cellar on the coast of Ross-shire, waiting for a lawyer’s clerk to decide whether they had value.

***

### IV. The Mechanics of Remembering

Why do we keep anything?

Before I took this commission, I had lived for eleven years in two rooms on the top floor of a tenement in Marchmont. I had a desk of fumed oak, four thousand books on the history of property law, and a woman named Clara who visited me on alternate Thursdays. 

We did not talk of marriage, nor did we talk of the future; we spoke of the small, dry particulars of our weeks. She worked in the registry of births and deaths, copying names from the ledger of the parish into the ledger of the county. Her hands were always clean, always faintly scented with carbolic soap and almond oil.

Then, one Thursday in the spring of my thirty-fifth year, she did not come. 

There was no note. A week later, I received a printed card from her brother, an ironmonger in Perth, informing me that Clara had died of an inflammation of the lungs after three days’ illness. 

When I went to her lodgings, the landlady had already cleared her room. Her clothes had been sold to a dealer from the Cowgate; her books had been taken by the deacon; her bed had been scrubbed with vinegar and rented to a telegraphist. I asked for something—a ribbon, a hairpin, a nib from her pen. The landlady, whose face had the greasy shine of mutton fat, looked at me with the suspicious dullness of her class.

"The brother took the silver," she said. "The rest went in the cart. If you’re wanting her trunk, it’s five shillings, but there’s naught in it but straw."

I did not buy the trunk. I walked back across the Meadows in the rain, my boots wet, and thought: *She has been subtracted without a remainder.* 

It was that idea—the absence of remainder—that had made my life in Marchmont impossible. A city is a great mill for the destruction of traces. It grinds its inhabitants into dust and uses the dust to mortar the next terrace of houses. The cobblestones are turned every forty years to present a fresh face to the hooves; the chimney pots are replaced; the names over the shops are painted out before the previous tenant is cold in the ground.

Finch’s house was the opposite of Marchmont. It was a place where no trace was permitted to disappear. 

Every morning, after my bowl of stirabout, I walked the length of the beach with a wicker creel on my back, as Finch had done for half a century. I found myself looking for things that had no business to exist: a child’s shoe of brown leather, its tongue torn out; a piece of deal board with three letters of a ship's name—*...MAR...*—branded into the grain; the brass casing of an artillery shell from some long-forgotten naval maneuver, stuffed with dried bladderwrack.

I brought them back. I washed them in rain-water from the butt—for salt must never dry on metal, it eats the marrow out of it—and laid them on the drying boards. 

I began to understand Finch’s handwriting. His notebooks were not records; they were litanies. He had realized that the tragedy of the world is not that things end, but that they are forgotten before they have finished ending. The world is full of things that are halfway through being destroyed, abandoned by their makers, by their owners, by their observers, left to finish the slow, humiliating business of dissolution in the dark.

He had offered them an audience. He had been their congregation of one.

***

### V. The Solitary Feast

By midwinter, the sun was no more than an orange thumb-mark pressed against the southern horizon for three hours at noon. The sea turned the color of lead, heavy and oily, rolling into the cove with a sluggish weight that smelled of dead weed and snow.

My provisions were running low. The salt beef was down to the gristle, and the meal had begun to harbor small, white weevils whose carapaces floated to the top of the pot when the water boiled. I skimmed them off with a wooden spoon and ate the porridge anyway; it tasted of lime and wet flour, but it was warm.

On the twenty-first of December—the shortest day—the wind dropped entirely. 

The silence that fell upon the Cape was thicker than the storm had been. For three months, my ears had been tuned to the roar of the water and the rattle of the sash-windows; now, suddenly, there was only the sound of my own lungs, the scrape of my pencil on the page, and the faint, dry ticking of the clockwork barograph on the mantle.

I went out onto the rocks. The sea was like a sheet of hammered tin, gray-white and completely flat, stretching away to the north until it disappeared into a bank of low, greasy fog.

There was no drift coming ashore. The tide had backed out to a distance I had never seen before, exposing reefs of black bladder-kelp that looked like the backs of drowned horses. 

I walked out beyond the high-water line, beyond the zone of shingle, down onto the shelf of blue clay that lay beneath the gravel. It was cold; the salt mud froze to the welts of my boots with a crackling sound like dry leaves.

There, in a hollow between two ribs of basalt, something caught the pale noon light.

It was an ordinary bottle of thick, greenish glass—a soda bottle, or perhaps a beer bottle from some provincial brewery—stoppered with a plug of wood that had been bound in oiled canvas and sealed with tallow.

Inside, clearly visible through the glass, was a roll of paper.

My hands began to shake. In three months, despite all Finch’s collections, I had never found a message in a bottle myself. Finch had found hundreds, but they had all been cataloged, dried, pinned out like dead moths. This was fresh. This had come through the fog, through the quiet water, had crossed the reef while I was boiling my meal, and had sat down here in the mud to wait for me.

I did not open it on the beach. I carried it back to the house as though it were made of thin ice, holding it against the wool of my coat.

I set it upon the table by the oil lamp. I did not immediately reach for the corkscrew or the pliers. I sat down and looked at it.

The glass was scored with hundreds of fine, hair-like scratches where it had tumbled against the sand of some distant bank. It had been in the sea a long time—months, perhaps years. A small colony of acorn barnacles had fixed themselves to the neck, their shells sharp and white as porcelain.

What did I want it to say?

Did I want it to be the coordinates of a sinking schooner, an account of three men starving on an island of guano, a scrap of scripture from a missionary lost off Labrador? Or did I want it to be Clara?

That was the absurdity, the disease of the Cape. I had begun to believe that this house was the terminal point of the universe, the place where all lines converged, where everything that had been lost in the world must eventually come ashore, provided one sat by the fire long enough and kept the lamps filled.

I took my pocketknife and cut through the tallow. The grease came away in pale, waxy flakes that smelled of mutton and lye. I worked the point of the blade under the wooden plug, rocking it until the wood groaned and came out with a dull *plop*, releasing an air that had been trapped inside for God knows how long.

It did not smell of the sea. It smelled of tobacco, dry paper, and the inside of a desk.

I tilted the bottle. The roll of paper slid forward, but caught on the shoulder. I took a pair of long watchmaker’s tweezers from Finch’s kit, reached in, and drew it out.

It was a single leaf of blue-lined ledger paper, torn from a pocket memorandum book. The message was written in pencil, in a small, tight, unpracticed hand, the letters pressed so hard into the paper that the lead had silvered:

*“We are fifty miles south of the Faroes. The coal is finished. We are burning the hatch-covers. The engine will not turn. If this is found by anyone, tell my mother at North Shields that I was not afraid, and that Jack gave me his mitts before he went over. The water is up to the fire-bars. 12 January 1904. Thomas Caine.”*

1904.

Ninety years.

The bottle had been ninety years in the water. It had drifted three thousand miles, perhaps four, circling the great gyre between Iceland, Greenland, and the Hebrides. It had drifted through two world wars; it had drifted while the coal trade died; it had drifted while the empire that had built the ship dissolved into ink and treaties; it had drifted while the boy’s mother turned to clay in a cemetery in North Shields, while Jack’s bones were scattered by the currents across the cod-banks, while Clara died in a room in Perth, while I grew old over legal parchment in Marchmont.

Ninety years to travel fifty miles south of the Faroes to this spit of black rock.

It had missed the boy’s mother. It had missed the boy’s century. It had arrived now, when there was no one left alive who had ever seen Thomas Caine’s face, or heard the sound of his voice when he was cold, or knew what color his eyes were.

I sat with the paper in my hand until the lamp went out. 

The kerosene was finished. The room grew black, save for the dull red glow of the stove damper and the faint, grey square of the window looking out upon the North Atlantic.

I did not write the slip for Item 21,411. 

I rolled the paper tight, slid it back into the green bottle, and pressed the wooden plug back into the neck. I did not seal it with wax. I walked down to the slipway, down over the slippery kelp, down to the edge of the water where the tide was beginning to make again, moving in with a low, sucking hiss over the stones.

I swung my arm and threw it as far as I could out into the black water.

There was no splash that I could hear—only the surge of the current as it took the weight of the glass, pulled it down into the trough, and carried it away toward the seam where the tides fight.

***

### VI. The Departure

Maro came three weeks later, in the second week of January, when the ice on the fresh-water butt had frozen three feet thick and I had been reduced to melting frost from the windowpanes to make my tea.

He stood in the doorway of the morning room, his oilskin coat stiff with frozen spray, his hat in his hand. He looked at the stacks of tea chests, the rows of shoes, the thousands of corks, the bottles of green and amber glass, the ledgers I had stacked neatly by the hearth.

"The lawyers in Edinburgh wrote to the factor," he said. He did not step inside; he knew the house was not a house, but a tomb that had been left open to the weather. "They said it isn’t worth the carriage. The auctioneer won’t come north of Inverness for old timber and scrap iron. They’re giving the ground to the Admiralty for a marker-beacon. They say you’re to take what’s yours and leave the key under the door."

"There is no key," I said.

He nodded, as though he had expected this. "The boat’s at the pier. The wind is coming round to the west. If we don’t go now, we won’t go till February."

I looked at my luggage. I had one small valise: two shirts, my spare boots, my razor, and my field notebooks. 

"Wait," I told him.

I went through the rooms one last time. I did not take the tortoiseshell comb. I did not take the letter about the herring and the bonnet ribbon. I did not take the rubber duck that had sailed around the pole.

I went to the Ballroom of Unsent Letters. The catgut strings had begun to sag under the weight of the frost that had crept through the broken sashes; the letters were stiff, coated in a fine, white fur of rime that turned them into small, hanging shields of silver.

I unhitched the catch on the great west window—the one that Julian Finch had built to look out upon the Minch—and pushed it wide.

The winter wind entered the room like an animal. It smelled of brine, snow, and the great, empty spaces between Scotland and the pole. 

It took the strings. For a moment, the room was filled with a dry, rustling music, like the sound of a thousand birds waking in an aviary. Then the catgut snapped. 

The papers did not fall; they rose. They were caught by the draft that sucked toward the chimney, swirled twice around the ceiling where the plaster angels were peeling, and then went streaming out through the open sash into the grey gale, scattering across the basalt, across the shingle, out into the white seam where the tides were meeting.

They looked like gulls. For three seconds, five seconds, they were indistinguishable from the birds that follow the herring boats, turning their white bellies to the squall, dipping into the troughs, rising over the crests.

Then the salt took them.

"Come on," Maro called from the foot of the stairs, his voice flat, impatient. "The tide’s making."

I shut the door behind me. I did not put the key under the stone; there was no lock that could have held against the water anyway. 

We rowed away from the spit with the current behind us. I did not look back at the house until we had cleared the point and the great swell of the open Minch took the dory by the keel, lifting us five feet into the cold light.

From there, *The Teeth* looked very small—only a thin, black finger of rock reaching out into the grey desert of the sea, holding up a handful of timber that was already beginning to lean toward the tide.

"It will be down by the spring," Maro said, not turning his head, his oars rising and falling in their rowlocks with that slow, indifferent rhythm that has nothing to do with hope.

"Yes," I said. "By the spring."

And I put my hands into my pockets, feeling the lint, the loose threads, the smooth, empty corners where nothing was preserved, and turned my face toward the shore.

By December, the weather had closed down like an iron trap. Maro came once, his dory leaping like a horse across the grey swells, his face lashed red by sleet. He did not come ashore; he merely brought the boat close enough to the slippery timber of the pier to toss two sacks of oats, a tin of dried yeast, and three boxes of salt beef onto the deck before hauling his sheet and falling away with the tide.

"Stay off the lower shingle!" he shouted through his cupped hands, his voice thin against the thrum of the wind. "The shelf is cutting out! The drift is coming in deep!"

I did not ask what he meant by *the drift coming in deep*. I knew already.

For a week, the wind had been blowing from the north-northeast, dragging the great polar water down through the gaps between the islands. At night, the house shuddered with a frequency that matched the long Atlantic rollers. In my bed, beneath three horsehair blankets and my wool greatcoat, I could feel the impact through the stone foundations: a thud that traveled up through the spine of the rock, through the floorboards, into the iron frame of the cot, shaking my heart against my ribs.

In the mornings, the beach had changed its face.

A storm on that coast is not a removal; it is an addition. The tide does not take away; it disgorges. It vomited up fields of kelp whose stalks were as thick as a man’s thigh, black and shining like rubber pipes; it threw up timbers of Norwegian spruce, splintered as though by siege-engines, their iron bolts turned to spikes of orange rust; it cast up the plastic debris of our own century, those bright, unrotting toys, bleach bottles with Spanish labels, crates from fish-packing plants in Halifax, nylon nets that had drifted across the pole like strangling veils.

Finch had spent the last decade of his life dealing with this modern flotsam, and his notes on it were marked by a profound, clinical disgust.

*“The ocean used to cast up bones,”* he had written in 1898, in the small, trembling script of his last months. *“Wood, horn, linen, wool, iron. Things that had been born of the earth and were slowly being unmade by the brine, returning by degrees to their elements. Now it casts up things that cannot die. They are not dead; they were never alive. They are the ghosts of oil. They will lie upon these stones when the sun has grown red and cold.”*

In the cellars of the house, where the water seeped through the mortar and stood three inches deep in the floor-gutters, he had arranged his collection of modern detritus: thousand upon thousand of plastic oil containers, sun-bleached to the color of bone; monofilament lines tangled like the hair of suicides; and, most strangely, hundreds of rubber bath toys—yellow ducks, blue frogs, pink pigs—which had been spilled from a container ship in the mid-Pacific in the early nineties and had circled the Arctic basin for five years before finding their way down the spout between Cape Vane and the mainland.

He had arranged them in rows on shelves made of driftwood, their painted eyes rubbed away by the pumice of the sand, their bills slightly parted in identical, molded smirks. 

They were utterly terrifying. They had crossed the roof of the world without a crew, without a thought, preserved in their bright, petrochemical innocence through months of pack-ice and months of midnight sun, to sit at last in this dark cellar on the coast of Ross-shire, waiting for a lawyer’s clerk to decide whether they had value.

***

### IV. The Mechanics of Remembering

Why do we keep anything?

Before I took this commission, I had lived for eleven years in two rooms on the top floor of a tenement in Marchmont. I had a desk of fumed oak, four thousand books on the history of property law, and a woman named Clara who visited me on alternate Thursdays. 

We did not talk of marriage, nor did we talk of the future; we spoke of the small, dry particulars of our weeks. She worked in the registry of births and deaths, copying names from the ledger of the parish into the ledger of the county. Her hands were always clean, always faintly scented with carbolic soap and almond oil.

Then, one Thursday in the spring of my thirty-fifth year, she did not come. 

There was no note. A week later, I received a printed card from her brother, an ironmonger in Perth, informing me that Clara had died of an inflammation of the lungs after three days’ illness. 

When I went to her lodgings, the landlady had already cleared her room. Her clothes had been sold to a dealer from the Cowgate; her books had been taken by the deacon; her bed had been scrubbed with vinegar and rented to a telegraphist. I asked for something—a ribbon, a hairpin, a nib from her pen. The landlady, whose face had the greasy shine of mutton fat, looked at me with the suspicious dullness of her class.

"The brother took the silver," she said. "The rest went in the cart. If you’re wanting her trunk, it’s five shillings, but there’s naught in it but straw."

I did not buy the trunk. I walked back across the Meadows in the rain, my boots wet, and thought: *She has been subtracted without a remainder.* 

It was that idea—the absence of remainder—that had made my life in Marchmont impossible. A city is a great mill for the destruction of traces. It grinds its inhabitants into dust and uses the dust to mortar the next terrace of houses. The cobblestones are turned every forty years to present a fresh face to the hooves; the chimney pots are replaced; the names over the shops are painted out before the previous tenant is cold in the ground.

Finch’s house was the opposite of Marchmont. It was a place where no trace was permitted to disappear. 

Every morning, after my bowl of stirabout, I walked the length of the beach with a wicker creel on my back, as Finch had done for half a century. I found myself looking for things that had no business to exist: a child’s shoe of brown leather, its tongue torn out; a piece of deal board with three letters of a ship's name—*...MAR...*—branded into the grain; the brass casing of an artillery shell from some long-forgotten naval maneuver, stuffed with dried bladderwrack.

I brought them back. I washed them in rain-water from the butt—for salt must never dry on metal, it eats the marrow out of it—and laid them on the drying boards. 

I began to understand Finch’s handwriting. His notebooks were not records; they were litanies. He had realized that the tragedy of the world is not that things end, but that they are forgotten before they have finished ending. The world is full of things that are halfway through being destroyed, abandoned by their makers, by their owners, by their observers, left to finish the slow, humiliating business of dissolution in the dark.

He had offered them an audience. He had been their congregation of one.

***

### V. The Solitary Feast

By midwinter, the sun was no more than an orange thumb-mark pressed against the southern horizon for three hours at noon. The sea turned the color of lead, heavy and oily, rolling into the cove with a sluggish weight that smelled of dead weed and snow.

My provisions were running low. The salt beef was down to the gristle, and the meal had begun to harbor small, white weevils whose carapaces floated to the top of the pot when the water boiled. I skimmed them off with a wooden spoon and ate the porridge anyway; it tasted of lime and wet flour, but it was warm.

On the twenty-first of December—the shortest day—the wind dropped entirely. 

The silence that fell upon the Cape was thicker than the storm had been. For three months, my ears had been tuned to the roar of the water and the rattle of the sash-windows; now, suddenly, there was only the sound of my own lungs, the scrape of my pencil on the page, and the faint, dry ticking of the clockwork barograph on the mantle.

I went out onto the rocks. The sea was like a sheet of hammered tin, gray-white and completely flat, stretching away to the north until it disappeared into a bank of low, greasy fog.

There was no drift coming ashore. The tide had backed out to a distance I had never seen before, exposing reefs of black bladder-kelp that looked like the backs of drowned horses. 

I walked out beyond the high-water line, beyond the zone of shingle, down onto the shelf of blue clay that lay beneath the gravel. It was cold; the salt mud froze to the welts of my boots with a crackling sound like dry leaves.

There, in a hollow between two ribs of basalt, something caught the pale noon light.

It was an ordinary bottle of thick, greenish glass—a soda bottle, or perhaps a beer bottle from some provincial brewery—stoppered with a plug of wood that had been bound in oiled canvas and sealed with tallow.

Inside, clearly visible through the glass, was a roll of paper.

My hands began to shake. In three months, despite all Finch’s collections, I had never found a message in a bottle myself. Finch had found hundreds, but they had all been cataloged, dried, pinned out like dead moths. This was fresh. This had come through the fog, through the quiet water, had crossed the reef while I was boiling my meal, and had sat down here in the mud to wait for me.

I did not open it on the beach. I carried it back to the house as though it were made of thin ice, holding it against the wool of my coat.

I set it upon the table by the oil lamp. I did not immediately reach for the corkscrew or the pliers. I sat down and looked at it.

The glass was scored with hundreds of fine, hair-like scratches where it had tumbled against the sand of some distant bank. It had been in the sea a long time—months, perhaps years. A small colony of acorn barnacles had fixed themselves to the neck, their shells sharp and white as porcelain.

What did I want it to say?

Did I want it to be the coordinates of a sinking schooner, an account of three men starving on an island of guano, a scrap of scripture from a missionary lost off Labrador? Or did I want it to be Clara?

That was the absurdity, the disease of the Cape. I had begun to believe that this house was the terminal point of the universe, the place where all lines converged, where everything that had been lost in the world must eventually come ashore, provided one sat by the fire long enough and kept the lamps filled.

I took my pocketknife and cut through the tallow. The grease came away in pale, waxy flakes that smelled of mutton and lye. I worked the point of the blade under the wooden plug, rocking it until the wood groaned and came out with a dull *plop*, releasing an air that had been trapped inside for God knows how long.

It did not smell of the sea. It smelled of tobacco, dry paper, and the inside of a desk.

I tilted the bottle. The roll of paper slid forward, but caught on the shoulder. I took a pair of long watchmaker’s tweezers from Finch’s kit, reached in, and drew it out.

It was a single leaf of blue-lined ledger paper, torn from a pocket memorandum book. The message was written in pencil, in a small, tight, unpracticed hand, the letters pressed so hard into the paper that the lead had silvered:

*“We are fifty miles south of the Faroes. The coal is finished. We are burning the hatch-covers. The engine will not turn. If this is found by anyone, tell my mother at North Shields that I was not afraid, and that Jack gave me his mitts before he went over. The water is up to the fire-bars. 12 January 1904. Thomas Caine.”*

1904.

Ninety years.

The bottle had been ninety years in the water. It had drifted three thousand miles, perhaps four, circling the great gyre between Iceland, Greenland, and the Hebrides. It had drifted through two world wars; it had drifted while the coal trade died; it had drifted while the empire that had built the ship dissolved into ink and treaties; it had drifted while the boy’s mother turned to clay in a cemetery in North Shields, while Jack’s bones were scattered by the currents across the cod-banks, while Clara died in a room in Perth, while I grew old over legal parchment in Marchmont.

Ninety years to travel fifty miles south of the Faroes to this spit of black rock.

It had missed the boy’s mother. It had missed the boy’s century. It had arrived now, when there was no one left alive who had ever seen Thomas Caine’s face, or heard the sound of his voice when he was cold, or knew what color his eyes were.

I sat with the paper in my hand until the lamp went out. 

The kerosene was finished. The room grew black, save for the dull red glow of the stove damper and the faint, grey square of the window looking out upon the North Atlantic.

I did not write the slip for Item 21,411. 

I rolled the paper tight, slid it back into the green bottle, and pressed the wooden plug back into the neck. I did not seal it with wax. I walked down to the slipway, down over the slippery kelp, down to the edge of the water where the tide was beginning to make again, moving in with a low, sucking hiss over the stones.

I swung my arm and threw it as far as I could out into the black water.

There was no splash that I could hear—only the surge of the current as it took the weight of the glass, pulled it down into the trough, and carried it away toward the seam where the tides fight.

***

### VI. The Departure

Maro came three weeks later, in the second week of January, when the ice on the fresh-water butt had frozen three feet thick and I had been reduced to melting frost from the windowpanes to make my tea.

He stood in the doorway of the morning room, his oilskin coat stiff with frozen spray, his hat in his hand. He looked at the stacks of tea chests, the rows of shoes, the thousands of corks, the bottles of green and amber glass, the ledgers I had stacked neatly by the hearth.

"The lawyers in Edinburgh wrote to the factor," he said. He did not step inside; he knew the house was not a house, but a tomb that had been left open to the weather. "They said it isn’t worth the carriage. The auctioneer won’t come north of Inverness for old timber and scrap iron. They’re giving the ground to the Admiralty for a marker-beacon. They say you’re to take what’s yours and leave the key under the door."

"There is no key," I said.

He nodded, as though he had expected this. "The boat’s at the pier. The wind is coming round to the west. If we don’t go now, we won’t go till February."

I looked at my luggage. I had one small valise: two shirts, my spare boots, my razor, and my field notebooks. 

"Wait," I told him.

I went through the rooms one last time. I did not take the tortoiseshell comb. I did not take the letter about the herring and the bonnet ribbon. I did not take the rubber duck that had sailed around the pole.

I went to the Ballroom of Unsent Letters. The catgut strings had begun to sag under the weight of the frost that had crept through the broken sashes; the letters were stiff, coated in a fine, white fur of rime that turned them into small, hanging shields of silver.

I unhitched the catch on the great west window—the one that Julian Finch had built to look out upon the Minch—and pushed it wide.

The winter wind entered the room like an animal. It smelled of brine, snow, and the great, empty spaces between Scotland and the pole. 

It took the strings. For a moment, the room was filled with a dry, rustling music, like the sound of a thousand birds waking in an aviary. Then the catgut snapped. 

The papers did not fall; they rose. They were caught by the draft that sucked toward the chimney, swirled twice around the ceiling where the plaster angels were peeling, and then went streaming out through the open sash into the grey gale, scattering across the basalt, across the shingle, out into the white seam where the tides were meeting.

They looked like gulls. For three seconds, five seconds, they were indistinguishable from the birds that follow the herring boats, turning their white bellies to the squall, dipping into the troughs, rising over the crests.

Then the salt took them.

"Come on," Maro called from the foot of the stairs, his voice flat, impatient. "The tide’s making."

I shut the door behind me. I did not put the key under the stone; there was no lock that could have held against the water anyway. 

We rowed away from the spit with the current behind us. I did not look back at the house until we had cleared the point and the great swell of the open Minch took the dory by the keel, lifting us five feet into the cold light.

From there, *The Teeth* looked very small—only a thin, black finger of rock reaching out into the grey desert of the sea, holding up a handful of timber that was already beginning to lean toward the tide.

"It will be down by the spring," Maro said, not turning his head, his oars rising and falling in their rowlocks with that slow, indifferent rhythm that has nothing to do with hope.

"Yes," I said. "By the spring."

And I put my hands into my pockets, feeling the lint, the loose threads, the smooth, empty corners where nothing was preserved, and turned my face toward the shore.
